limitations: The NASA-TLX results were potentially confounded by a learning effect due to the unbalanced experimental design (participants always experienced the temperature setback condition after the control condition). (Section 4.1, p.11)
A limited number of Emotiv Insight and Empatica E4 wristbands were available, leading to EEG and HR data being analyzed from only 12 out of 19 subjects. (Section 2.3.3, p.5)
Heart Rate Variability (HRV) data was not adopted for analysis due to the E4 wristband's infrequent sampling rate and many missing data occurrences. (Section 2.3.3, p.5)
Relative humidity was not independently controlled during the experiment. (Section 3.1, p.6)
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the effects of a higher summer temperature setpoint (25 °C vs. 22 °C) on office workers' cognitive load and thermal comfort in a controlled climate chamber. Findings indicated that cognitive performance, as measured by Cambridge Brain Science tests, was not significantly affected by the temperature change. While NASA-TLX showed a significant reduction in cognitive load at 25 °C, the authors attributed this to a learning effect rather than temperature, a conclusion supported by EEG and heart rate data which showed no significant difference between temperature conditions. Participants' thermal comfort was not significantly jeopardized, with acceptability remaining above 80% at 25 °C, although perceived air quality decreased and preference for more air movement increased. A key limitation was the potential confounding learning effect due to the unbalanced experimental design, particularly for NASA-TLX results, and the small sample size for physiological data.
